Poster for the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition

Joost Schmidt’s railway-station poster joins the school’s name, the dates, and the signet into one diagonal figure of circles, squares, and bars.

Source
Bauhaus Kooperation: Plakat zur Bauhaus-Ausstellung in Weimar 1923
Creator
Joost Schmidt
Made
1923
Style
Bauhaus (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Constructive, bold, geometric
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the Bauhaus-Archiv image published by Bauhaus Kooperation (710 × 1016 px). This copy has the later overprint that moves the opening to 15 August. Also compared the smaller Commons copy, which shows the first state with “Juli–Sept”.
Reviewed
25 September 2026
Rights
Open license, stored. License: public domain. Rights policy

Context

Schmidt made the design for a competition. It is a cross of circles and squares set on the diagonal, and it contains Oskar Schlemmer’s Bauhaus signet, which the competition brief required. Bauhaus Kooperation.

The first version advertised the exhibition in 120 German railway stations with the dates July to September. A sticker later updated the dates. Bauhaus Kooperation.

The Museum of Modern Art holds a copy as “Staatliches Bauhaus Ausstellung,” 1923. MoMA 6235.

Observed

  • A red ring at upper left and a large black half-disc at lower right sit at the ends of a thick black diagonal band.
  • Rectangles in black, red, and stippled gray overlap at right angles along the band.
  • “STAATLICHES BAUHAUS” runs above the ring; “AUSSTELLUNG”, “WEIMAR”, and “1923” follow the diagonal.
  • The capitals are hand-drawn and angular, built from straight strokes and small arcs.
  • A small version of the Schlemmer signet sits inside the red ring.
  • A pink overprint strip reads “Eröffnung verschoben auf 15. Aug – 30. Sept”.
  • The ground is unprinted off-white paper. Wide empty margins surround the central figure.

Why it belongs

The poster shows the change from the expressionist early Bauhaus to constructive geometry. Type and shapes form one system: the words follow the same diagonal as the bars.

The palette is red, black, and gray, not the full primary triad. This reduced red-and-black version is common in Bauhaus print work.

Borrow

Build a heading and its shapes into one diagonal figure, and let the words follow the edges of the shapes.

Use one saturated accent with black and a textured gray, and leave wide margins of plain ground.
